"'''The Way It Is'''" is a song by American rock group [[Bruce Hornsby#The Range|Bruce Hornsby and the Range]]. It was released in July 1986 as the second single from their debut album, ''[[The Way It Is (Bruce Hornsby album)|The Way It Is]]''. The song topped the charts of Canada, the Netherlands, and the United States while entering the top 20 in at least eight other countries, including Australia, Ireland, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. Written by [[Bruce Hornsby]], it made explicit reference to the [[Economic Opportunity Act]], also known as the 1964 Poverty Act, as well as the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]]. Hornsby referred to it as a "song about [[racism]]."<ref name="Afterlife">{{Cite web|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/bruce-hornsby-interview-way-it-is-non-secure-connection-1036032/|title=Bruce Hornsby on the Hip-Hop Afterlife of 'The Way It Is' and His Posthumous Leon Russell Duet|first=David|last=Browne|date=August 3, 2020|work=Rolling Stone |access-date=August 27, 2025}}</ref>

"The Way It Is" is a song by American rock group Bruce Hornsby and the Range. It was released in July 1986 as the second single from their debut album, The Way It Is. The song topped the charts of Canada, the Netherlands, and the United States while entering the top 20 in at least eight other countries, including Australia, Ireland, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. Written by Bruce Hornsby, it made explicit reference to the Economic Opportunity Act, also known as the 1964 Poverty Act, as well as the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Hornsby referred to it as a "song about racism."

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: In 1985, working by himself in his garage in [[Van Nuys]], California, Hornsby wrote the lyrics for "The Way It Is" first, after which he developed the song's music and created the song's piano [[lick (music)|lick]].<ref name="Bronson">{{cite book |last=Bronson |first=Fred|title=The Billboard Book of Number One Hits | edition=5th | publisher=[[Billboard Books]]| page=655 |location=New York |year=2003|isbn=978-0823076772}}</ref> The song later appeared on a [[Demo (music)|demo recording]] made by Hornsby that included "[[Mandolin Rain]]" and "The Red Plains". This tape led to him being signed by [[RCA Records]] in 1985.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.routemagazine.us/stories/a-conversation-with-bruce-hornsby|title=A Conversation with Bruce Hornsby | ROUTE Magazine|website=www.routemagazine.us}}</ref>
sections.text: In 1985, working by himself in his garage in Van Nuys, California, Hornsby wrote the lyrics for "The Way It Is" first, after which he developed the song's music and created the song's piano lick. The song later appeared on a demo recording made by Hornsby that included "Mandolin Rain" and "The Red Plains". This tape led to him being signed by RCA Records in 1985.

sections.heading: Song lyrics and music
sections.wikitext:
The song documents racism that Hornsby encountered in the [[American South]] growing up in [[Williamsburg, Virginia]]. He said that the song was "about growing up in the sixties in a small town with narrow-minded, provincial attitudes." He specifically cited memories of individuals in the town disparaging [[Martin Luther King Jr.]], saying "not everyone in Williamsburg felt like that, of course – certainly my parents didn't - but it was the prevailing attitude."<ref name="DeMain">{{Cite web |last=DeMain |first=Bill |date=September 17, 2026|title=How a Bruce Hornsby song about racism in the South became an unlikely No. 1 |url=https://www.loudersound.com/bands-artists/bruce-hornsby-and-the-range-the-way-it-is |access-date=September 18, 2026 |website=Louder}}</ref>

The song features a 50 second intro, lyrics referencing the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Act]] and two piano solos.<ref name="DeMain"/> Speaking to ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' in 2020, Hornsby provided his perspective on the song, saying that it was "a wonderful accident, a great fluke. A song about racism with two improvised solos is hardly the formula for pop success then or at any time."<ref name="Afterlife" />

When discussing the song with Steve Pond in a different interview published in ''[[Rolling Stone]]'', Hornsby expressed his belief that "The Way It Is" was not conventionally commercial, adding that it was "a very even-running song" that "doesn't reach the highs and lows that I think of as desirable".<ref name="Bronson"/> He later described "The Way It Is" as "a novelty record" that "connected" with people "even if it was totally uncommercial", and that it "sounded so different than anything else".<ref name=Liner>{{Cite AV media notes |last=Graff |first=Gary |title=[[Greatest Radio Hits]] |year=2003 |type=Liner Notes |publisher=RCA|location=United States}}</ref>

The song features a 50 second intro, lyrics referencing the Equal Employment Opportunity Act and two piano solos. Speaking to Rolling Stone in 2020, Hornsby provided his perspective on the song, saying that it was "a wonderful accident, a great fluke. A song about racism with two improvised solos is hardly the formula for pop success then or at any time."

When discussing the song with Steve Pond in a different interview published in Rolling Stone, Hornsby expressed his belief that "The Way It Is" was not conventionally commercial, adding that it was "a very even-running song" that "doesn't reach the highs and lows that I think of as desirable". He later described "The Way It Is" as "a novelty record" that "connected" with people "even if it was totally uncommercial", and that it "sounded so different than anything else".

sections.heading: Release
sections.wikitext:
"The Way It Is" initially attained commercial success in the United Kingdom.<ref name=Liner/> Prior to its official release as a single, [[BBC Radio 1]] had played the song 22 times and was placed on the station's A list. British DJ [[Gary Davies]] had referred to the song as "the best record I've heard in [[wiktionary:yonks|yonks]]".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=July 26, 1986 |title=Which Single |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1986/Music-Week-1986-07-26.pdf#page=10 |access-date=September 25, 2026 |magazine=[[Music Week]] |page=10}}</ref> It was officially released as a single in July 1986 by RCA Records. All editions of the UK single included "The Red Plains", with the [[twelve-inch single]] also featuring "The Wild Frontier".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=July 26, 1986 |title=New Singles |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1986/Music-Week-1986-07-26.pdf#page=95|access-date=September 25, 2026 |magazine=[[Music Week]] |page=28}}</ref> Commenting on the song's popularity in the United Kingdom, Hornsby mentioned that "Everyone thought it should have been a B side, but then [[BBC Radio 1]] played it and, boom, there it went. The last place it hit was in the United States."<ref name="Afterlife" />

In the United States, "The Way It Is" initially broke on [[album-oriented rock]] radio stations. By September 12, 1986, 63% of all album-oriented rock stations reporting to ''[[Radio & Records]]'' had included the song on their playlists.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=September 12, 1986 |title=AOR Tracks {{!}} Breakers |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Archive-RandR/1980s/1986/RR-1986-09-12.pdf#page=140|access-date=September 25, 2026|magazine=[[Radio & Records]] |page=140 |via=World Radio History}}</ref> The following month, a [[music video]] was released to accompany the single. It was filmed on a London rehearsal stage, was directed by Gerard de Thame and produced by Helen Langridge.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Moleski |first=Linda |date=October 11, 1986 |title=Video Track |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/80s/1986/BB-1986-10-11.pdf |access-date=December 2, 2025 |magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |page=56 |via=World Radio History}}</ref>
sections.text:
"The Way It Is" initially attained commercial success in the United Kingdom. Prior to its official release as a single, BBC Radio 1 had played the song 22 times and was placed on the station's A list. British DJ Gary Davies had referred to the song as "the best record I've heard in yonks". It was officially released as a single in July 1986 by RCA Records. All editions of the UK single included "The Red Plains", with the twelve-inch single also featuring "The Wild Frontier". Commenting on the song's popularity in the United Kingdom, Hornsby mentioned that "Everyone thought it should have been a B side, but then BBC Radio 1 played it and, boom, there it went. The last place it hit was in the United States."

In the United States, "The Way It Is" initially broke on album-oriented rock radio stations. By September 12, 1986, 63% of all album-oriented rock stations reporting to Radio & Records had included the song on their playlists. The following month, a music video was released to accompany the single. It was filmed on a London rehearsal stage, was directed by Gerard de Thame and produced by Helen Langridge.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext: Andy Gill wrote in ''[[NME|New Musical Express]]'' that the song was "one of those rare cases where melancholia and euphoria shift subtly back and forth in constant elision, complementing the blend of hope and resignation in the lyrics."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Gill |first=Andy |date=October 25, 1986 |title=Bruce Hornsby: The Virginian |url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/bruce-hornsby-the-virginian |access-date=December 2, 2025 |url-access=subscription |magazine=[[NME|New Musical Express]] |via=Rock's Backpages}}</ref> ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' said that the song combined [[roots rock]] with "articulate commentary".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=September 20, 1986 |title=Singles |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ayQEAAAAMBAJ&printsec=frontcover&rview=1&lr=#v=onepage&q&f=false |access-date=December 2, 2025 |magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |page=73 |via=Google Books}}</ref> ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' called the song "sensitive and wonderfully produced" and thought that it "should bring attention to Hornsby’s overlooked but worthy debut LP of the same name."<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=September 13, 1986 |title=Single Releases |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1986/CB-1986-09-13.pdf |access-date=December 2, 2025 |magazine=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]] |page=9 |via=World Radio History}}</ref> ''[[The Chicago Tribune]]'' labeled it as "a moody pop/rock song with a social message as powerful as its melodic line."<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 12, 1986 |title=Bruce Hornsby's Range Finds a Home In No. 1 Spot |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1986/12/12/bruce-hornsbys-range-finds-a-home-in-no-1-spot/ |access-date=September 17, 2026 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]]}}</ref>
sections.text: Andy Gill wrote in New Musical Express that the song was "one of those rare cases where melancholia and euphoria shift subtly back and forth in constant elision, complementing the blend of hope and resignation in the lyrics." Billboard said that the song combined roots rock with "articulate commentary". Cashbox called the song "sensitive and wonderfully produced" and thought that it "should bring attention to Hornsby’s overlooked but worthy debut LP of the same name." The Chicago Tribune labeled it as "a moody pop/rock song with a social message as powerful as its melodic line."

sections.heading: Sampling and other usage
sections.wikitext:
The song has been sampled by various rappers such as [[E-40]] for his song "[[Things'll Never Change]]",<ref>{{Citation |title=E-40 - Things'll Never Change (Official Video) ft. Bo-Rock |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_UBEBLRu-Y |access-date=December 20, 2021 |language=en}}</ref> by [[Tupac]] for [[Changes (Tupac Shakur song)|"Changes"]], by DJ [[Don Diablo]] for his song "Never Change", and [[Polo G]] for "[[Wishing for a Hero]]" in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hiphopdx.com/news/id.16830/title.bruce-hornsby-talks-approving-2pacs-song-changes|title=Bruce Hornsby Talks Approving 2Pac's Song "Changes"|first=Omar|last=Burgess|date=September 12, 2011|website=HipHopDX}}</ref> According to Hornsby, Polo G had planned on booking an airplane to meet with him and ask for permission to sample "The Way it Is". After hearing the sampled track from Polo G's management, Hornsby reached out to the artist and authorized him to use the song in "Wishing for a Hero".<ref name="Afterlife"/>

A few years after the release of Hornsby's original version, [[Coretta Scott King]] asked permission from Hornsby to use the song for the [[King Center for Nonviolent Social Change]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Tannenbaum |first=Rob |date=September 22, 1988 |title=Bruce Hornsby's Southern Comforts |url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/bruce-hornsbys-southern-comforts |access-date=December 2, 2025 |url-access=subscription |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |via=Rock's Backpages}}</ref>
sections.text:
The song has been sampled by various rappers such as E-40 for his song "Things'll Never Change", by Tupac for "Changes", by DJ Don Diablo for his song "Never Change", and Polo G for "Wishing for a Hero" in 2020. According to Hornsby, Polo G had planned on booking an airplane to meet with him and ask for permission to sample "The Way it Is". After hearing the sampled track from Polo G's management, Hornsby reached out to the artist and authorized him to use the song in "Wishing for a Hero".

A few years after the release of Hornsby's original version, Coretta Scott King asked permission from Hornsby to use the song for the King Center for Nonviolent Social Change.
